For a digital marketing agency in Pune running Google Ads for a local business, the two settings that most often waste budget are not keywords or bids. They are location targeting and the ad schedule. Choose the locations people really travel from, make sure the "who sees your ad" option matches your business, exclude the places you cannot serve, and run ads only in the hours when somebody can answer the phone. Done properly, these settings stop a Pune clinic or a coaching class paying for clicks from a visitor in another city who was never going to become a customer. This guide explains how to set each option, how to decide between a radius and a list of areas, how to build an ad schedule from your own data, and how to check the settings after launch.

It is written for owners who pay for Google Ads, either directly or through an agency, and want to understand what they are paying for. It is deliberately about settings and judgement, not about promises. We do not quote click prices or conversion rates for Pune, because they differ by category and season, and any figure offered without your account data is a guess.

## Why Location Settings Decide Who You Pay For

Google Ads decides who can see an ad by matching the search with the locations you chose. When the match is looser than your real service area, you pay for clicks from people you cannot serve. When it is tighter, you miss people who would have come. Both errors are invisible unless you look, because the account still shows impressions, clicks and a cost per click that looks reasonable.

The most common problems we see in small-business accounts are these.

- The campaign is targeted at "India" or "Maharashtra" because the setup wizard offered it, while the business serves three neighbourhoods.
- The default option shows ads to people who are merely interested in a location, not only to those who are in it.
- Locations that cannot be served, such as a different city with the same locality name, are not excluded.
- Ads run at night when no one answers the phone, and the leads arrive to a missed call.

Each of these has a simple fix, covered below.

## Choosing the Targeting Option: Presence or Interest

Google Ads lets you choose how people are matched to your locations. The wording and defaults have changed over the years, so check the current settings screen in your account, but the underlying choice is stable.

- **Presence:** people who are in, or regularly in, your targeted locations.
- **Presence or interest:** people in the locations plus people who show interest in them, for example by searching for them or viewing pages about them.
- **Search interest:** people who search for or show interest in the location, whether or not they are in it. This is relevant mostly to tourism and similar businesses.

For a business that serves customers at a physical location or in a defined area, such as a Pune dentist, a salon, a plumber or a school, the narrower presence option is usually the better starting point. People interested in Pune but living elsewhere may be future relocators or researchers, but for an urgent local service they rarely convert, and you would be paying for them.

There are exceptions where interest matching helps. A hotel, a wedding venue, a tour operator or a hospital that attracts patients from other cities may want people who are researching Pune from elsewhere. A university or coaching institute might want families planning a move. The test is whether a person who is not in Pune can still become your customer. If yes, include them; if no, keep to presence.

Google's help documentation describes these options and says which one is the default for new campaigns. Read the current page before you set anything, because the product has changed these labels before.

## Radius or Named Areas?

Google Ads gives three ways of setting where to advertise: named locations (cities, districts, pincodes), a radius around a point, and location groups. For local service businesses the choice that matters is between a radius and named areas.

### When a radius works

A radius around your premises suits a business whose customers come to you: a clinic, a gym, a restaurant, a retail shop. Choose the distance from how far people actually travel, which you can find from your own customer records. Look at where your last hundred customers live, plot them roughly and see where the real boundary lies. In a city like Pune, the effective distance varies greatly by direction and by traffic. A five-kilometre radius across a river or a congested corridor may represent a longer journey than ten kilometres along a clear road.

A radius is imprecise. It ignores boundaries that matter to customers, such as municipal limits or the line between Pune and Pimpri-Chinchwad, and it may include areas you do not serve.

### When named areas work better

A business that travels to customers, such as a plumber, an electrician, a pest control service or a home tutor, should target the areas it serves by name. You can add specific localities or postal codes as separate locations, so the account matches your real service map. This also helps reporting, because the location report then shows clearly which areas bring enquiries and which do not.

### A practical method

1. List every area you serve, by name, from your customer records and your service calendar.
2. Rank them by the number of enquiries or jobs in the last six to twelve months.
3. Start with the top areas that account for most of your work.
4. Add farther areas later, after the first ones have proven profitable, rather than all at once.
5. Review the location report each month and adjust.

If you are new and have no records, begin with a modest radius around your premises or office and expand according to what the data shows.

### Exclusions

Add excluded locations for places you cannot or do not want to serve. Examples include another city that shares a name with a Pune locality, a district beyond your delivery limit, or a region where your licence does not apply. Exclusions prevent wasted clicks that a positive list does not catch.

## Location Bid Adjustments: Use Them Sparingly

Google Ads allows you to raise or lower bids for specific locations. With automated bidding, such as the strategies we discuss in our article on [smart bidding for lead generation](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-google-ads-smart-bidding-lead-generation-2026), the system already considers location signals, and manual adjustments may conflict with it. Use location bid adjustments only when you have good data showing that an area performs differently, and review them regularly. If one area produces clearly better leads, a separate campaign for it often gives clearer control and reporting than a stack of adjustments.

## Building an Ad Schedule From Your Own Data

An ad schedule tells Google Ads to show ads, or adjust bids, on certain days and hours. Its value depends entirely on what your business does with the lead.

### The case for scheduling

If your enquiries arrive by phone and nobody is available at night, ads at 11 pm generate clicks and, at best, a missed call. A schedule that limits call-focused ads to staffed hours means you pay for calls you can answer. If your enquiries arrive through a form that you can answer next morning, running all hours may be fine, provided your follow-up is fast; our article on [lead response speed](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-lead-response-speed-follow-up-workflow-2026) explains why.

### The case against hasty scheduling

Switching ads off at certain hours can also remove some of your best customers. Many people search for a clinic, a school or a contractor late in the evening and call or enquire the next morning. If your tracking only records immediate calls, those people look worthless when they are not. Before cutting any hours, check the data in the right way.

### How to decide hour by hour

1. Collect at least several weeks of data, longer if your volume is low. Short windows exaggerate noise.
2. Look at the hour-of-day and day-of-week reports for clicks, cost, conversions and cost per conversion.
3. Use conversions that reflect real leads, such as qualified calls, form submissions confirmed by the server and WhatsApp enquiries, rather than every click. See our guide to [tracking phone calls from Google Ads](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-google-ads-call-tracking-phone-leads-2026) and the article on [lead quality and offline conversions](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-lead-quality-offline-conversions-2026).
4. Compare hours by cost per qualified lead, not by clicks.
5. Lower bids or pause in hours with persistently poor results, but only where you have enough conversions to trust the pattern.
6. Review again after a month, and after seasonal changes.

Remember the account's time zone setting. A schedule uses the time zone of the account, so confirm that it is set to India Standard Time.

### Call-only and phone-led businesses

If the business depends on phone calls, align the schedule with the hours when calls are answered and use call assets that respect the schedule. Also consider whether the click-through path allows the visitor to enquire out of hours, perhaps through a form or WhatsApp, so that a night-time searcher has a way to reach you.

## Matching Ads and Landing Pages to the Location

Settings alone do not make an ad local. The message and the destination should show that you serve the person's area.

- Mention the city or the neighbourhoods in the headlines or descriptions where it is truthful and natural, such as "Dentist in Kothrud".
- Add location assets so that your address and map pin appear with the ad.
- Send people to a page that confirms the service area and shows how to reach you, rather than a generic homepage.
- Keep the business name, address and phone number identical to your Google Business Profile and website. Our article on [local citations and directory listings](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-local-citations-justdial-sulekha-directory-listings-2026) covers consistency.

Be careful with location pages on your website. Creating one near-identical page for every locality is a doorway-page tactic that search engines treat as low-quality. Our guide to [service-area pages and doorway pages](/blog/website-designer-pune-service-area-location-pages-doorway-2026) explains how to do it properly.

## Checking the Settings After Launch

A campaign set up correctly can still drift as you add or edit things. Check the evidence rather than the settings alone.

### The location reports

In Google Ads, the locations report shows the places that triggered your impressions and clicks, split by where people were and where they showed interest, where available. Use it to find clicks from places you did not intend. If a surprising area appears, check the targeting option and add an exclusion.

### The search terms report

People often type the location into the search. A report showing terms with other cities' names tells you that the matching is wider than you want. Add those places as negatives or exclusions. The process mirrors what we describe in our article on [search terms and negative keywords](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-search-terms-negative-keywords-2026).

### A monthly checklist

1. Is the targeting option still "presence" (or your deliberate choice)?
2. Are the target areas current, and are exclusions still correct?
3. Do the location report and search terms show clicks from outside the service area?
4. Does the ad schedule match staffed hours and the hours that brought real leads?
5. Is the account time zone correct?
6. Do the ads and landing pages mention the right locations?
7. Are phone numbers and addresses in assets identical to the website and Business Profile?

## A Worked Example With Assumed Numbers

This example uses invented numbers to show the reasoning. They are not Pune benchmarks.

Imagine a physiotherapy clinic in Baner with a monthly Google Ads budget of ₹30,000. It is targeting "Pune" with the presence or interest option and running all day. Over a month the report shows 600 clicks and 18 enquiries that the front desk recorded, an effective cost of about ₹1,670 per enquiry. Looking deeper, the clinic finds that:

- About a fifth of the clicks come from outside the city, and none of those became appointments.
- Phone calls between 9 pm and 7 am went unanswered; the ads still cost money in those hours.
- Nearly all booked patients live within about 8 kilometres.

The fix is a radius of 8 kilometres around the clinic, presence targeting, exclusions for the other cities that appeared, and a schedule that shows call-focused ads from 8 am to 8 pm while keeping the form-based ad group active at night with a "we reply by 9 am" promise.

Suppose the next month shows 400 clicks and 20 enquiries. That would be ₹1,500 per enquiry, but you cannot conclude the settings alone caused it. Seasonality, ad copy and competitors all change. The honest conclusion is that the account now spends less on clicks that never could have converted, and the right measure is the cost per qualified appointment over several months.

## Mistakes That Waste Budget

- Leaving the wizard's default country or state targeting untouched.
- Using the broader interest option for a business that cannot serve people elsewhere.
- Cutting night-time hours on the basis of last-click data when the leads arrive the next morning.
- Adding locations in bulk without watching performance by area.
- Layering many bid adjustments on top of automated bidding.
- Making a landing page that does not mention the area, so the visitor wonders if you are local.
- Reviewing the campaign monthly in aggregate and never opening the location report.

## What to Ask an Agency

When you evaluate a proposal from a digital marketing agency, these questions reveal how carefully they will manage location and timing.

- Which targeting option will you use, and why?
- How will you decide the service area, radius or named list?
- Which exclusions will you add on day one?
- What will you report by location, hour and day?
- How will you treat calls and form leads that arrive outside business hours?
- Who has access to the account, and can we see the settings directly?

An agency that answers specifically, using your customer data, is thinking about your business. An agency that answers with generic assurances is not. Our article on [what to expect from a retainer](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-retainer-deliverables-reporting-2026) lists what regular reporting should include.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the best location targeting setting for a local business in Google Ads?
For a business that serves people in a defined area, targeting people who are in or regularly in that area (the presence option) is usually the better starting point, because the broader interest option can show ads to people who live elsewhere. Check the current labels in your account, and use the interest option only if people outside the area can become customers.

### Should I use a radius or a list of areas for my Pune business?
Use a radius around your premises if customers travel to you, and a list of named localities or pincodes if you travel to them. Base the radius on where your actual customers live, and review the location report monthly.

### Can I run Google Ads only during business hours?
Yes, with an ad schedule. It helps most when your leads come by phone and nobody answers after hours. Decide from your own hour-by-hour data, using real conversions rather than clicks, because some customers search at night and enquire the next day.

### Why am I getting clicks from other cities?
Common causes are a broad location setting, the interest-matching option, a locality name shared with another city, or searches that include another place. Check the locations and search terms reports, then tighten the option and add exclusions or negative keywords.

### Do location bid adjustments help?
Sometimes, when you have clear data that one area performs better or worse. With automated bidding they can conflict with the system, so use them sparingly, or create a separate campaign for the area that deserves its own budget and reporting.

## Where to Start

Open your Google Ads account today and look at three things: the targeting option on each campaign, the location report for the last 30 days, and the hour-of-day report. In half an hour you will know whether you are paying for people you cannot serve. Fix the targeting option and exclusions first, since that is the quickest and least risky change, and make any schedule change only after you have enough conversion data.
